author: A Robot
objectives: Students will identify and name the four chambers of the heart, the four heart valves, and the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
Students will trace the path of blood through the heart's dual circulation, naming each chamber, valve, and vessel in order.
Students will distinguish the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit and explain why the right and left sides of the heart serve different circulatory functions.

Students will explain why the left ventricle has a substantially thicker myocardium than the right ventricle, relating wall thickness to the pressure required to perfuse the systemic versus pulmonary circuits.
Students will describe the function of the atrioventricular and semilunar valves in preventing backflow, and identify which valves separate which chambers or chamber-vessel pairs.

modules.moduleName: Scene 1: Exterior Heart Anatomy and Orientation
modules.description: Students view a full-size human heart in anatomical position with an intact exterior model and a cutaway cross-section side by side. The scene introduces gross orientation, major vessels, and the perspective reversal that occurs when viewing anatomical structures from the patient's own frame of reference.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Understand the anatomical orientation of the heart in the thoracic cavity
Identify the major vessels entering and leaving the heart on the exterior surface
Grasp the reason anatomical 'right' and 'left' are reversed from the viewer's perspective

components.text: Heart Anatomy: Exterior View & Interior Structure

clips.changeMeaning: Establishes the scene with two heart models and contextualizes the anatomical perspective convention.
clips.narration: Welcome to cardiac anatomy. You are viewing the human heart in its anatomical position: apex pointing downward and slightly to the left, with the base at the top. On your left is an intact heart showing the external surface and the major vessels. On your right is a cutaway view that exposes the internal chambers and structures. Notice that the heart's 'right side' appears on your left, and the 'left side' appears on your right. This reversal occurs because anatomical directions are always described from the patient's perspective, not the observer's. You can rotate both models to examine them from any angle.

clips.changeMeaning: Narration identifies and explains the major vessels visible on the exterior heart.
clips.narration: On the exterior heart, you can identify five major vessel groups. The superior vena cava and inferior vena cava enter from the top and bottom, bringing deoxygenated blood from the head, body, and limbs. The pulmonary trunk emerges from the front of the heart and splits into left and right pulmonary arteries, carrying deoxygenated blood to the lungs. The pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the posterior surface. Finally, the aorta emerges from the top and curves upward to distribute oxygenated blood throughout the entire body. These vessels represent the entry and exit points for the dual circulation loops we will explore in detail.

modules.moduleName: Scene 2: Guided Structural Tour of the Heart
modules.description: A comprehensive walkthrough of the heart's internal architecture, progressing through chambers, valves, and major vessels with labels and simultaneous highlighting of corresponding external landmarks.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the four chambers by their anatomical names and position
Locate and name the four valves and describe their positions between specific structures
Map internal chambers and valves to external landmarks on the intact heart

components.text: Structural Tour: Chambers, Valves, and Vessels

clips.changeMeaning: Sets context for the guided structural identification tour.
clips.narration: Now we will take a guided tour of the heart's internal structures. We will examine each chamber, each valve, and each major vessel in sequence. As we highlight each structure inside the cutaway view, watch how it corresponds to features on the exterior surface. This mapping will help you understand how internal chambers connect to external landmarks.

clips.changeMeaning: Activates and positions a label for chamber identification during narration.
clips.narration: We begin with the four chambers. The right atrium is a thin-walled chamber at the top-right of the heart; it receives blood from the systemic veins. Below it is the right ventricle, a thick-walled chamber that pumps blood to the lungs. On the left side, the left atrium is a thin-walled chamber at the top-left that receives blood from the pulmonary veins. Below it is the left ventricle, a very thick-walled chamber that pumps blood to the entire body. Notice that the left ventricle is visibly thicker than the right ventricle—this structural difference reflects their different functional demands.

clips.changeMeaning: Narration describes the four valves, their positions, and dual nomenclature for the mitral valve.
clips.narration: Next are the four valves. The tricuspid valve separates the right atrium from the right ventricle; it has three leaflets. The pulmonary valve sits between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk, allowing blood to exit the right heart toward the lungs. On the left side, the mitral valve—also called the bicuspid valve because it has two leaflets—separates the left atrium from the left ventricle. The aortic valve sits between the left ventricle and the aorta, allowing oxygenated blood to exit toward the body. The mitral and bicuspid terms are equivalent; both names appear in clinical practice.

clips.changeMeaning: Narration completes the structural tour by identifying the major vessels and their roles.
clips.narration: Finally, the major vessels. The superior vena cava enters the right atrium from above, bringing blood from the head and upper body. The inferior vena cava enters the right atrium from below, bringing blood from the lower body and abdomen. The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to both lungs. The pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. The aorta emerges from the left ventricle and arches upward to distribute oxygenated blood throughout the systemic circulation. These five vessels are the highways of the circulatory system.

modules.description: A dynamic visualization of blood flow through the heart's chambers and vessels using color coding: blue for deoxygenated blood and red for oxygenated blood. Students observe the continuous, steady-state flow of dual circulation.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Understand the color-coding convention for deoxygenated and oxygenated blood
Observe the continuous dual-circuit flow through both pulmonary and systemic pathways
Distinguish the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit based on blood oxygenation status

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces the color-coding convention and prepares students for observing continuous flow.
clips.narration: Now we will watch blood flow through the heart using a color-coding system. Blue represents deoxygenated blood returning from the tissues of the body, seeking oxygen. Red represents oxygenated blood that has picked up oxygen in the lungs and is ready to deliver it throughout the body. The heart continuously pumps blue blood to the lungs and red blood to the body, maintaining two synchronized loops of circulation.

clips.changeMeaning: Plays continuous blood flow animation through the entire dual-circuit pathway with narration.
clips.narration: Watch as blue blood enters the right atrium from the veins of the body. The right atrium contracts, pushing blood through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. The right ventricle then contracts, pumping blue blood through the pulmonary valve and out through the pulmonary arteries to the lungs. In the lungs, the blood picks up oxygen and becomes red. Red blood returns via the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. The left atrium contracts, pushing blood through the mitral valve into the left ventricle. The left ventricle contracts powerfully, pumping red blood through the aortic valve and out through the aorta to supply the entire body. The body tissues consume the oxygen, the blood becomes blue again, and it returns through the veins to the right atrium. This cycle repeats continuously.

clips.changeMeaning: Distinguishes the pulmonary and systemic circuits by their functions and blood color patterns.
clips.narration: The dual circulation has two distinct circuits. The pulmonary circuit is the shorter loop: blue deoxygenated blood flows from the right atrium through the right ventricle to the lungs, then returns as red blood to the left atrium. This circuit delivers blood to the lungs for gas exchange. The systemic circuit is the longer loop: red oxygenated blood flows from the left atrium through the left ventricle to the body through the aorta, supplies tissues with oxygen, and returns as blue deoxygenated blood through the veins to the right atrium. This circuit delivers oxygen to every cell in the body. Together, these two circuits form the complete pattern of human circulation, continuously driven by the pumping action of the heart.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4: Step-by-Step Red Blood Cell Trace
modules.description: An interactive single-cell journey through the complete circulation. A user-controlled red blood cell moves one step at a time through each chamber, valve, and vessel, with labels and narration describing what happens at each step.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Sequence the complete path of blood through both pulmonary and systemic circuits
Understand the functional purpose of each cardiac chamber and valve during the cell's journey
Recognize the transition from deoxygenated to oxygenated blood and the sites where gas exchange occurs

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces the interactive cell-tracing experience and establishes starting position.
clips.narration: You are now following a single red blood cell on its complete journey through the heart and circulation. The cell begins in the superior vena cava, carrying deoxygenated blood from the upper body. Press the Next button to advance the cell one step at a time through the entire circuit. At each step, you will see the cell move to a new location, and narration will describe what is happening in the heart's structures.

clips.changeMeaning: Cell advances through right atrium, tricuspid valve, right ventricle, and pulmonary valve with narration.
clips.narration: The red blood cell enters the right atrium through the superior vena cava along with additional blood from the inferior vena cava. The right atrium contracts, pushing the cell through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. The right ventricle then contracts, pushing the cell through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk. The cell travels through the pulmonary arteries toward the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: Cell reaches lungs, changes color from blue to red as it oxygenates.
clips.narration: In the lung capillaries, the red blood cell releases its accumulated carbon dioxide into the alveoli and picks up fresh oxygen from inhaled air. The cell changes color from blue to red as it becomes oxygenated. Oxygen-rich blood now returns to the heart through the pulmonary veins.

clips.changeMeaning: Cell enters left side of heart and exits through aorta to systemic circulation.
clips.narration: The oxygenated red blood cell enters the left atrium through the pulmonary veins. The left atrium contracts, pushing the cell through the mitral valve into the left ventricle—a thick, muscular chamber. The left ventricle contracts powerfully, pushing the cell through the aortic valve into the aorta, which distributes it throughout the systemic circulation to supply oxygen to all tissues of the body.

clips.changeMeaning: Cell completes its journey and returns to starting position, cycle restarts.
clips.narration: The cell delivers its oxygen to body tissues and becomes deoxygenated again, turning blue. Deoxygenated blood is collected by systemic veins and returns to the superior vena cava, where our cell is now rejoining the circulation. The complete cycle has taken approximately 60 seconds in the living heart at rest. The loop repeats continuously with each heartbeat.

modules.moduleName: Scene 5: Wall Thickness Asymmetry in the Ventricles
modules.description: A comparative cross-sectional view showing the pronounced thickness difference between right and left ventricular walls, with scale markers and functional explanation for the structural asymmetry.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare the relative wall thickness of the right and left ventricles
Understand that wall thickness reflects the pressure demands of each circuit
Explain why the left ventricle must be substantially thicker than the right ventricle

components.text: Ventricular Wall Thickness: Form Reflects Function

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces the side-by-side cross-sectional comparison and calls attention to the thickness difference.
clips.narration: One of the most striking structural features of the heart is the asymmetry in wall thickness between the two ventricles. You are viewing cross-sections of the right and left ventricles cut at the same level through the center of the heart. The cross-sectional areas show the myocardial wall—the muscular tissue that contracts to pump blood. Notice immediately that the left ventricular wall is substantially thicker than the right ventricular wall.

clips.changeMeaning: Explains the physiological basis for ventricular wall thickness asymmetry.
clips.narration: This thickness difference is not random—it reflects the different functional demands placed on each ventricle. The right ventricle pumps blood a short distance to the lungs, a low-pressure circuit requiring only enough force to overcome the resistance of the pulmonary vessels and capillaries. In contrast, the left ventricle must pump blood throughout the entire body against much higher vascular resistance. To generate the pressure needed to perfuse tissues in the head, limbs, abdomen, and all internal organs, the left ventricular wall must be approximately two to three times thicker than the right. This structural adaptation is a perfect example of how cardiac anatomy is shaped by functional requirements. When disease weakens the left ventricle—or when chronic hypertension forces it to generate even higher pressures—the ventricular wall can thicken further, a response called left ventricular hypertrophy.

modules.moduleName: Scene 6: Valve Function and Backflow Prevention
modules.description: An examination of how the four valves function to prevent backward flow of blood, with visual demonstration of open and closed states during the cardiac cycle.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Categorize valves into atrioventricular and semilunar types and name the valves in each category
Understand how each valve opens and closes during different phases of the cardiac cycle
Explain the structural and functional consequence of valve malfunction

components.text: Ventricular Contraction: AV valves CLOSED, Semilunar valves OPEN

Atrioventricular (AV) Valves: Tricuspid & Mitral
Semilunar Valves: Pulmonary & Aortic

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces the two valve categories and their anatomical positions.
clips.narration: The four valves of the heart are one-way gates that ensure blood flows in the correct direction and never backward. We classify them into two functional categories: the atrioventricular or AV valves—the tricuspid and mitral valves—sit between atria and ventricles and prevent backflow into the atria. The semilunar valves—the pulmonary and aortic valves—sit between ventricles and their outflow arteries and prevent backflow into the ventricles. Each valve opens and closes in response to pressure changes during the cardiac cycle.

clips.changeMeaning: Explains AV valve mechanics during the cardiac cycle.
clips.narration: During ventricular relaxation, blood fills the atria and pushes the AV valve leaflets open, allowing atrial blood to flow into the ventricles. When the ventricles contract, pressure inside the ventricles rises sharply. This pressure pushes the AV valve leaflets closed and prevents blood from flowing backward into the atria. The tricuspid valve has three leaflets; the mitral valve has two. Papillary muscles and chordae tendinae—tendon-like cords—anchor the leaflets and prevent them from flipping too far backward. If these structures fail, blood regurgitates backward during ventricular contraction, reducing the efficiency of forward flow.

clips.changeMeaning: Explains semilunar valve mechanics during the cardiac cycle.
clips.narration: The semilunar valves operate differently. During ventricular contraction, high ventricular pressure pushes the semilunar valve leaflets open, allowing blood to exit the ventricles into the pulmonary trunk and aorta. When the ventricles relax and ventricular pressure drops below arterial pressure, blood begins to flow backward toward the ventricles. The backward flow pushes the semilunar valve leaflets closed. The pulmonary and aortic valves each have three leaflets, and when closed, they meet and seal the opening completely, preventing any blood from leaking backward into the ventricles. Without functional semilunar valves, diastolic blood pressure would rise and forward flow would be reduced.

clips.changeMeaning: Summarizes the coordinated valve function during the complete cardiac cycle.
clips.narration: During ventricular contraction, the AV valves are closed and the semilunar valves are open, allowing the ventricles to pump blood forward into the arteries. During ventricular relaxation, the AV valves open and the semilunar valves are closed, allowing the ventricles to fill with blood from the atria. This coordinated opening and closing of all four valves ensures unidirectional flow and efficient pumping. Any structural damage to valve leaflets or their supporting structures compromises this function and leads to heart murmurs, valve regurgitation, or stenosis—conditions that reduce cardiac output and systemic perfusion.

modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Correctly identify all four chambers by their anatomical names
Recognize all four valves and distinguish between atrioventricular and semilunar categories

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces the quiz and explains the format and objectives.
clips.narration: You have now learned the anatomy of the heart in detail. This quiz will test your ability to identify structures by name. A structure will be highlighted on the heart model. Four candidate names will appear on the screen. Select the correct name from the options. After each selection, you will receive feedback. The quiz cycles through all chambers, valves, and major vessels. Try to achieve a perfect score to demonstrate your mastery of cardiac anatomy.

clips.changeMeaning: Presents a sample structure identification question for student practice.
clips.narration: A chamber is highlighted. Is this the: A) Right Atrium, B) Right Ventricle, C) Left Atrium, or D) Left Ventricle? Select the correct answer.

modules.description: A sequenced quiz where students trace blood flow through the circulation, naming the next chamber or vessel in the pathway based on a given starting position.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Sequence the complete path of blood through the cardiac cycle and circulation
Distinguish between pulmonary and systemic circuits and their distinct oxygen content
Recognize the atypical oxygenation of pulmonary arteries and veins compared to systemic vessels

components.text: Blood has just entered the Right Atrium. What is the next chamber or vessel in the path?
Select an answer from the options

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces the blood flow quiz and highlights a common source of confusion.
clips.narration: This quiz tests your understanding of the complete blood flow pathway through the heart and circulation. You will be given a starting position—for example, blood in a specific chamber or vessel—and asked to name the next structure in the pathway. The quiz progresses through the entire dual-loop circulation. Pay close attention to the difference between pulmonary and systemic vessels, especially the fact that pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood and pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood—the opposite pattern of systemic circulation.

clips.changeMeaning: Presents a sample blood flow tracing question to begin the interactive quiz.
clips.narration: Blood has just entered the right atrium from systemic veins. What is the next chamber it flows into? Your options are: A) Right Ventricle, B) Left Atrium, C) Pulmonary Artery, or D) Aorta. Select the correct next structure in the pathway.

modules.moduleName: Scene 9: Lab Recap and Concept Summary
modules.description: A concluding summary that reviews the five core concept areas covered throughout the lab: structural inventory, dual circulation, blood cell journey, ventricular asymmetry, and valve function.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Synthesize the five major concept areas into a coherent understanding of cardiac anatomy and physiology
Relate structural features to functional outcomes in the cardiovascular system
Prepare for clinical application of cardiac anatomy knowledge

components.text: Lab Recap: Key Concepts in Cardiac Anatomy

1. STRUCTURAL INVENTORY
Chambers: Right atrium & ventricle, Left atrium & ventricle
Valves: Tricuspid, Pulmonary, Mitral/Bicuspid, Aortic
Major Vessels: Superior/Inferior vena cava, Pulmonary arteries/veins, Aorta

2. DUAL CIRCULATION
Pulmonary Circuit: Right atrium → Right ventricle → Lungs → Left atrium
Systemic Circuit: Left ventricle → Body → Systemic veins → Right atrium

3. BLOOD CELL JOURNEY
Deoxygenated → Right heart → Lungs (oxygenation) → Left heart → Oxygenated to body

4. VENTRICULAR ASYMMETRY
Left ventricle wall (10–15 mm) is 2–3× thicker than right (3–5 mm)
Reason: Left ventricle must overcome systemic resistance; right only pulmonary resistance

5. VALVE FUNCTION
Atrioventricular valves (Tricuspid, Mitral): Prevent backflow into atria during ventricular contraction
Semilunar valves (Pulmonary, Aortic): Prevent backflow into ventricles during relaxation

clips.changeMeaning: Opens the recap with a welcoming summary statement.
clips.narration: You have completed a comprehensive exploration of cardiac anatomy and the circulatory pathways it supports. We have examined the heart's structure in detail and traced the dual-loop circulation that it drives. Let us now review the five major concept areas that form the foundation of your understanding.

clips.changeMeaning: Narrates a comprehensive review of all five major concept areas and their clinical significance.
clips.narration: First, the structural inventory: four chambers, four valves, and five major vessels that comprise the anatomical scaffold of the heart. Second, the dual circulation: a pulmonary loop that oxygenates blood in the lungs and a systemic loop that delivers that oxygen throughout the body. Third, the complete journey of a red blood cell through this dual circulation, from deoxygenated return to the right atrium all the way through oxygenation and systemic delivery and back again. Fourth, the structural asymmetry of the ventricles—the left ventricle's substantially thicker wall reflects its greater functional demand, pumping against systemic resistance rather than the lower pulmonary resistance. And fifth, the elegant function of the four valves in maintaining unidirectional flow, with atrioventricular valves closing during contraction and semilunar valves closing during relaxation. Together, these five concepts explain not just what the heart is made of, but why it is built the way it is and how every structural feature serves a physiological function. This understanding is foundational for clinical practice in nursing, medicine, and all health professions.
